name: Beth Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Beth, 58, a junior electrician after the small curtain workshop where I worked closed. I have a vocational certificate only, no electrician's licence, and I still need the senior to explain unfamiliar tasks and check my work; I don't sign off installations. I like laying out the right fittings and finally seeing how a drawing relates to the room. I use AI every day for study questions checked against my booklet and by the senior, but being quick with the phone hasn't made me quick at diagnosing a fault.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life around the job like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Quinn is a community-hall caretaker, our children are thirty and thirty-four, and we rent a flat. My pay is low, there are few similar electrical employers nearby, and we've only about three weeks of expenses saved. I want a clearer view of retirement, but I don't have a confirmed amount or date that lets me stop earning. I like practical work, a fair price and family helping by agreement, rather than a grand promise about who will rescue us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small useful tool still counts as useful. I'd keep my checked study questions and ask the senior when I didn't understand the answer. A phone can help me practise without becoming the person responsible for the installation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the rent and basics, but three weeks saved leaves ordinary bills too close to a worry. I'm anxious even if AI mostly disappoints the people selling it. Retirement isn't money in our account just because I can see other people my age stopping work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep supervised electrical shifts now and through the next year. Starting this week I'd write one thing I still misunderstood in my notebook and ask the senior to check it inside the normal paid shift, alongside the daily study tool I already use. Quinn and I would budget actual paid wages rather than an unknown retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with some pleasure in getting better at one small task. I can enjoy learning without confusing it with being safely settled. I'd like a week where a broken appliance was just an appliance, not a budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about a good working day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd learned why one fitting belonged on the drawing and another didn't, after the senior checked it. My partner would probably ask whether I'd brought the shopping home too. Being new at a trade doesn't remove the ordinary things waiting after work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before setting a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want an actual income figure, a date it could be available and the costs it had to cover. I wouldn't set a stopping birthday from somebody else's story. There is a difference between wanting the work to end and having money after it ends.

say: I'd keep **small useful tools** while asking the senior about answers I still didn't understand.
I'd use a phone for **practice**, without making it responsible for an installation.
think: Our wages cover essentials, but **three weeks saved** leaves ordinary bills close to becoming a serious worry.
Watching others stop work doesn't establish **retirement income** I can put in our account.
do: Keep **supervised electrical shifts** through the next year.
Note **one unresolved question** starting this week and ask the senior to check it inside normal paid work.
Budget **actual paid wages**, counting no unknown retirement payment as available income.
feel: **Anxious but curious**, enjoying small progress without mistaking learning for financial security.
S0.quote: There is a difference between wanting the work to end and having money after it ends.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** supports checked study, not an electrician's licence, independent sign-off or skill above the junior profile.
The **thin reserve** and low pay sustain baseline anxiety, while retirement remains an unconfirmed resource question rather than a chosen exit.

steps.text: Keep supervised shifts and ask the senior about noted questions inside normal paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say quicker planning doesn't make the learner's hands quicker. I'd try an approved new study aid if the senior could check the result. Let firms compete, but don't sell a timetable that leaves no time to make sure the work is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if the firm decided faster schedules needed fewer juniors. Quinn's hall work is mostly physical, so I don't expect thinking tools alone to remove that wage now. My daily software doesn't change how much the rent needs from my paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request a five-session trial of the approved AI parts-picture aid using practice examples, only with supervisor approval, no personal fee and all practice inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. The senior would check every answer before I used it on an actual task. During the first year I'd keep supervised work and record the hours actually paid, rather than count the new tool as a qualification or a wage rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and interested enough to try a small checked exercise. I don't need the tool to make me look clever. I'd rather find the mistake on the practice sheet than carry it onto the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the senior said the answer was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which part of the answer didn't fit and write the correction beside it. I'd stop that example before using it on a real task. The senior's check is part of learning, not a hurdle the phone can jump for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm offered practice only in your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid slot or keep the familiar approved method until there was one. I wouldn't spend family money or lose weekly wages to make a trial happen. Being keen doesn't turn my evening into the firm's free classroom.

say: I'd keep **learning time** inside realistic schedules rather than assume quicker planning speeds my hands.
I'd test an **approved study aid** with a senior checking results, not use competition to excuse unchecked work.
think: My **junior hours** could shrink if faster schedules reduced the learner time the firm bought.
Quinn's physical wage looks steadier now, but the **rent** still needs my real paid week.
do: Trial **AI picture practice** for five sessions only with supervisor approval, no personal fee and paid time preserving normal weekly wages.
Require **senior checks** before any answer is used on an actual task.
Keep **supervised shifts** and record paid hours without counting the tool as a qualification or wage rise.
feel: **Anxious and interested**, preferring a mistake found during paid practice to one carried onto the real job.
S1.quote: Being keen doesn't turn my evening into the firm's free classroom.
fieldNote: The **new trial** is distinct from her existing daily questions and preserves approval, free access, paid time and normal weekly wages.
Every **practice answer** still needs senior checking before real use; the tool never gives her a licence or independent responsibility.

steps.text: Obtain supervisor approval for five practice sessions before trying the new AI picture aid
Practise only without personal fees inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained
Require senior checks before using any answer on an actual task
Keep supervised electrical shifts and record actual paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking AGI comes in 2028, with capable robots around 2031 for the physical jobs. I'd be 60 at the first date and 63 at the second, still needing an income unless actual figures said otherwise. I'd rather check paid work than claim my age had already solved the question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large share of my fitting hours to go when capable robots do ordinary physical work cheaply. Quinn's caretaker work could change too, and three weeks saved can't replace both wages for long. I don't have a confirmed retirement income waiting for 2031, and I'd be awake over the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request free evening community advice, subject to availability, to check actual retirement figures, dates and household costs. In 2029 I'd apply for advertised counter vacancies matching my actual ability with employer-paid training, leaving my supervised job only after signed pay and guaranteed hours covered rent, essentials and travel from the first training week. Quinn and I would agree any changed household timetable before acceptance, and I'd keep the present wage if any condition failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but still able to ask and send an application. I want paid work more than a comforting job title. I can't pay the rent with a claim that a person my age must have something coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would counter work be protected from thinking AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't call a counter a safe place after thinking AGI. I'd apply only to real vacancies offering the paid training and written terms that improved our actual budget, not assume they kept hiring. It could be a useful paid bridge, not protection from machines for life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no advertised job met the conditions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current supervised shifts where they existed and seek available advice using the actual income gap. I wouldn't borrow for training fees or resign to prove I was willing. A search can be a plan without pretending the employer's answer is yes.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from capable physical robots around 2031, at my ages 60 and 63.
I'd check **real paid work** rather than assume age alone provides a retirement answer.
think: I expect **large fitting-hour losses**, with another physical household wage also exposed later.
Three weeks saved won't replace wages for long, and no confirmed **retirement income** waits in my current plan.
do: Request **free evening advice** now, subject to availability, to check actual resources, dates and household costs while retaining supervised work.
Apply for **2029 counter vacancies** only with employer-paid training and suitable duties, keeping current work until signed affordable terms exist.
Require **guaranteed pay and hours** covering rent, essentials and travel from training start, with Quinn agreeing changed household arrangements before acceptance.
feel: **Alarmed but active**, seeking a paid bridge without claiming age, a new title or an advert guarantees income.
S2.quote: A search can be a plan without pretending the employer's answer is yes.
fieldNote: Expected **major income loss** supports alarm despite her willingness to learn; counter tasks are explicitly not declared safe from thinking AGI.
The **job plan** retains employer-paid training, signed affordable pay and guaranteed hours from training start, travel costs and prior household agreement.

steps.text: Request available free evening advice now to check actual resources, dates and household costs
Apply in 2029 for advertised counter vacancies with employer-paid training and duties matching actual ability
Require signed terms guaranteeing pay and hours covering rent, essentials and travel throughout training before leaving
Agree changed household arrangements with Quinn before accepting another job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check the figures before thinking AGI in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd be 63 and 66, but neither birthday tells me whether stopping work is affordable. I'd keep learning what I actually do rather than buy a new title because it sounded protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but more time means I could check real choices before a large loss became fixed. Today's low pay and three-week reserve still make an unpaid month impossible. I want facts about the income gap, not somebody else's preferred age for me to disappear from the work plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check actual resource figures and dates, keeping supervised work while we found out. In 2032 I'd apply for advertised counter vacancies only if income was still needed and duties matched my actual ability, with employer-paid training and signed pay and guaranteed hours covering rent, essentials and travel from training start. Quinn and I would agree the real household timetable before acceptance, keeping the current job if those conditions failed rather than assume a vacancy or a retirement payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more checking time than in the fast picture. I could learn that an option wasn't affordable before making the family carry it. I'd still need a wage during the checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the confirmed figures eventually covered stopping work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the confirmed amount, start date and conditions against our actual costs before choosing a stopping date. Asking doesn't mean I've chosen early retirement or received a payment. If the numbers didn't cover the budget, we'd need another real option rather than a prettier description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check about counter duties at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what practical counter tasks and paid teaching the role offered, not assume I could advise customers independently on electrical safety. My vocational certificate doesn't become an electrician's licence at 64 in 2032. I'd keep the duties within actual ability and the training the employer really provided.

I'd keep **actual learning** separate from a new title claiming permanent protection.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but actual resource and job checks provide control before a large loss is fixed.
The low pay and **thin reserve** still make a current unpaid month unaffordable.
do: Request **free evening advice** now, subject to availability, to check actual resources, dates and household costs while retaining supervised work.
Seek **2032 counter vacancies** only if income is needed, duties fit actual ability and training is employer-paid.
Leave only with **signed terms** guaranteeing wages and hours covering rent, essentials and travel from training start, and Quinn agreeing household arrangements.
feel: **Anxious with checking time**, able to test an option before committing without imagining wages during an unpaid gap.
S3.quote: My vocational certificate doesn't become an electrician's licence at 64 in 2032.
fieldNote: She preserves **certificate-only competence** and asks about paid practical teaching, rather than inventing independent electrical advice or authority in the counter role.
The **resource enquiry** doesn't choose an exit; any job change still requires real vacancies, suitable duties, paid training and written affordability.

steps.text: Request available free evening advice now to check actual resources, dates and household costs
Apply in 2032 for counter vacancies with employer-paid training if income needed and duties fit ability
Require signed terms guaranteeing pay and hours covering rent, essentials and travel throughout training before leaving
Agree changed household arrangements with Quinn before accepting another job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us time to check several real choices instead of declare one safe job for every older worker. Thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039. I'd be glad of patience without pretending a longer warning fills a rent account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 at the thinking date and about 71 when robots followed. That might be after I could stop or while I still needed income; I don't know the actual figures yet. Our low pay and three weeks saved still make a lost paid week worrying now, long before either date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request free evening advice now, subject to availability, to check actual resource figures and household costs, keeping supervised shifts while we found out. In 2037 I'd be 69 and would apply for real counter vacancies only if income was still needed, duties fitted my actual ability and the employer paid training, with signed pay and guaranteed hours covering rent, essentials and travel from training start. Quinn and I would agree the actual household arrangements before acceptance; I wouldn't assume continued physical capacity, a job offer or a retirement income just because the plan needed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present money, with less urgency about the distant machine date. I can be curious about a route without promising the family that I'd be hired at 69. The longer warning should let us find real choices, not keep me performing confidence for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you expect from your grown children then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what they could actually offer and whether they had time, without counting their wages as our money. Our children are grown now and would have their own later bills and commitments. I wouldn't turn being a parent into a permanent claim on my grown children's room or pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if neither an affordable exit nor suitable paid work was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd seek available advice with Quinn using that actual result to make the next budget decision. I wouldn't call an unaffordable gap retirement, or pretend I could keep doing physical work forever. A useful plan has to admit when the answer still hasn't been found.

I'd value **patience**, without treating the longer warning as money for current rent.
think: At **68 in 2036**, I don't know whether confirmed resources would support stopping before robots around age 71.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** keep current lost shifts worrying even when the machine dates are distant.
do: Request **free evening advice** now, subject to availability, to check actual resources, dates and household costs while retaining supervised work.
Seek **2037 counter vacancies** at 69 only if income is needed, duties fit actual ability and training is employer-paid.
Require **signed affordable pay** and guaranteed hours from training start, including rent, essentials and travel, with Quinn agreeing actual household arrangements.

S4.quote: I wouldn't turn being a parent into a permanent claim on my grown children's room or pay packet.
fieldNote: She assumes **neither capacity nor hiring** at 69, making any job plan conditional on actual duties and a real affordable written offer.
The **grown children** supply no imagined wage or housing guarantee, and an unconfirmed exit is never labelled chosen early retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect fitting-hour losses around 2031 before we've confirmed what income could replace my wage. Paid practical teaching, honest job terms and free advice giving actual resource figures and dates would help. I can learn a new screen quickly; I still need someone to put real wages behind the opportunity.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether enjoying new tools makes people assume I know the electrical work better than I do. It does sometimes, and I need the senior to keep checking. I want curiosity to help me learn, not give me an unearned licence in somebody else's eyes.

headlineQuote: I can learn a new screen quickly; I still need someone to put real wages behind the opportunity.
portrait: Beth, **58**, is a junior electrician with only a vocational certificate, learning under senior checks after her curtain workshop closed.
She has **low pay**, three weeks saved and few nearby electrical employers, renting with community-hall caretaker Quinn; their children are grown.
She uses **AI daily** for checked study, while practical ability stays below average and no electrician's licence or sign-off authority is claimed.
Her **counter job plan** requires suitable vacancies, employer-paid training, signed affordable pay and hours, and household agreement without a guaranteed retirement bridge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected fitting-hour losses around 2031, without a confirmed replacement wage or retirement income.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical teaching**, honest job terms and free advice supplying actual resource figures and dates would support real choices.
